York’s own Martin Van Buren, a native Dutch speaker. Brooklyn is named for Breukelen in Utrecht, and Harlem is named for Haarlem in North Holland. New York defines itself as somewhat distinctive from the rest of the United States of America and chooses to do so specifically with reference to a certain notion of Dutch-ness. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I don’t think he bought it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This was an interesting experience for me, though, because it was a powerful reminder of the extent to which these national or sub-national identities are simultaneously very real and also totally made up. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Imagined communities</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are such things as historical facts. But the idea of history is linked to the idea of storytelling. Good history should be accurate (or at least avoid inaccuracy), but it also involves narrative choices that are beyond questions of fact. </p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I read John Keay’s “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a88f3b85-1878-4ed0-ba9f-6435e97bccae?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">India: A History</a><span>” recently and it starts with the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/795f59a2-0d07-482b-a732-95503989373d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Indus Valley civilization</a><span>, whose main population centers are in what’s now Pakistan. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Part of why he does this is that trying to tell the history of the specific geography of contemporary India wouldn’t make any sense. The lines that were drawn on a map in 1947 corresponded to real divisions within the Indian subcontinent that had existed in some form or another for hundreds of years, but the precise geography of contemporary “India” is completely ahistorical and reflects a lot of midcentury happenstance. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The story of India has to include the story of the British Raj and the Mughal Dynasty and the Maurya Empire and a dozen other things, none of which correspond exactly to the borders of today’s India. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tracing it all the way back to Moenjodaro is, I think, the kind of thing where you could have gone either way as an author. There’s little known about the Indus Valley people because their writing hasn’t been deciphered, and it seems like the Sanskrit language and the foundations of Hinduism </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2621c282-f982-4068-9a88-f5331d3295d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">come from outside the subcontinent</a><span>. I might have told the story in a different way that starts with the Indo-Aryan migration. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But what Keay is choosing to do is to tell the story in more the way that corresponds to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2621c282-f982-4068-9a88-f5331d3295d5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">how contemporary Indians construct</a><span> their national identity. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And that’s fair enough; people have to make choices about these things. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here in the United States, we clearly trace “our” political and cultural history to the British colonists. Even in the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0682fd0a-22cf-4e4e-abb6-b563aa763f68?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">subculture that does land acknowledgments</a><span>, the structure is that “we” (the descendants of British colonists) are acknowledging that “they” (the descendants of the Native Americans who lived there before the colonists arrived) were here first. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In most cases, of course, the speaker will not be actually descended from either group. But the founders of the country are our (metaphorical) fathers who brought forth on this continent a new nation that we belong to, while the indigenous peoples who were here first are other nations. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Indians, by contrast, do not see the Vedic conquerors (or the Mughals or the British) as the founding fathers of the nation — their nation goes all the way back to the first identifiable civilization in the area. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is all a long lead-in to say it’s notable that New York City clearly considers Peter Stuyvesant, the final director-general of New Netherland, to be among its Founding Fathers. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4294869a-ad25-4e40-8458-bee6e3edc530?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Peter Stuyvesant Little League</a><span> that plays pretty close to the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/974ec78b-2031-487a-a6a3-f35e0236b707?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Stuyvesant Town</a><span> mega-development. A little ways away from all that, you can find Stuyvesant Street — the only street in Manhattan that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2192f322-419e-437f-a303-d8a179b9686f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">actually runs from east to west</a><span> — and over in Brooklyn the Stuy in Bed-Stuy is Stuyvesant. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You absolutely </span><em>could </em><span>say that New York as a political community derives from England or that it derives from the Lenape, but generations of New Yorkers have chosen to define themselves as the heirs to New Netherland. And if Stuyvesant is ever canceled and has his name removed from all this stuff, it will be because of entanglements with the slave trade, not because New Yorkers decide to side with the English people who beat him rather than the Dutch guy who lost. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The legacy of Dutch values</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In terms of values, the key thing is that the Netherlands was a haven of religious toleration at a time when most of Europe was governed by a principle of state religions. </p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The Thirty Years’ War ended with the concept that each German prince could pick whichever religion he wanted and impose that on his little state. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Henry IV won the French Wars of Religion and became king, but found he had to convert to the Catholic faith to consolidate power. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The English Civil War, which had a strain of liberal parliamentarism versus absolute monarchy, ended with Oliver Cromwell establishing a theocratic regime. </p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the 17th century Netherlands was a land of toleration. The country’s origins relate to Protestants rebelling against their Habsburg overlords, but, having secured their independence, the Dutch did </span><em>not</em><span> establish a Cromwell-style Calvinist autocracy. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The Pilgrims who founded New England fled religious persecution in England and went to the Netherlands before migrating to America. Sephardic Jews expelled from Spain moved to the Netherlands, and later they were joined by Ashkenazi refugees from the Thirty Years’ War. The oldest continuously functioning Jewish congregation in the United States is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dca6b08a-6204-4d45-b9d9-b0d4a5c8abf3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Congregation Shearith Israel</a><span>, which was founded by Sephardic Jews who were living in Brazil. They came to Brazil during a brief period of Dutch rule, but after the Portuguese reconquered it they had to go somewhere, so they went to New Amsterdam. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Interestingly, Stuyvesant — the director general of the whole New Netherland at the time — was actually against this and tried to prohibit them from settling. But they appealed to the Dutch East India Company and he was overruled. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Anyone familiar with the standard patriotic narrative of the United States has probably heard that the country as a whole was founded by various religious dissenters and that tolerance and pluralism are hallmarks of the country that are enshrined in the Bill of Rights. If you visit the Jefferson Memorial or go to Monticello in Charlottesville, you’ll hear a lot about Thomas Jefferson’s role in all this. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the specific narrative I was taught in </span><em>New York</em><span> is that several of the original 13 colonies were founded in a spirit of religious particularism (Massachusetts for Puritans, Maryland for Catholics, Pennsylvania for Quakers) and New York — uniquely — was founded on the Dutch principle of religious tolerance. </span></p><p class="button-wrapper" 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I always remember this interaction because the Dutch guy’s incredulity was genuine, but it also genuinely shocked me at the time. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I had never really thought in an analytical way about the claim that New Yorkers are tolerant as a legacy of Dutch values — I took it for granted. But the Dutch had no idea what I was talking about; they were jealous of the concept of an American Way. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And there’s something to that. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If New York City can kinda sorta make up a distinct narrative about itself based on facts about the Netherlands, so can the Netherlands itself. The New Amsterdam values of my youth, at the end of the day, are really just the same broad values that liberals tend to ascribe to the United States as a whole. The difference is maybe just that the United States in the 1980s was a broadly more politically conservative place and the Walter Mondale/Michael Dukakis voters of New York City felt a little alienated from it. So they told themselves they were being Dutch. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a little bit fake but it’s obviously based on strands of truth. And I think there’s something constructive about it. The Dutch guy was right, after all, that it’s easier to promote assimilation if you give people something to assimilate to. And probably every nation can come up with some broadly factual way to associate itself with praiseworthy values and then claim those values as its own and define being a good member of the community partly in terms of expressing those values. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">You can’t just go buck wild and make stuff up that has no grounding in facts or it won’t be credible (and you’ll be associating your national identity with the non-praiseworthy value of lying). But it’s also not necessarily a question of accuracy-maxxing — you’re trying to tell a story. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">America as a whole has some pretty good stories that we can tell about ourselves, and I think we ought to tell them. Positive European stories would necessarily be somewhat different, but they’re still out there, waiting to be told. </p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" I’ll have more on this tomorrow. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Really shocking decisions handed down by the Supreme Court. There were a couple that were not awful. Lisa Graves gets to stay at the Federal Reserve, although that in itself is a huge contradiction to the important stuff that the court did. I mean, Lisa is important and the Fed is important, but much more important is Humphrey’s Executor, which is the generations-long precedent that says that when Congress creates an independent agency, it is independent. It’s able to make decisions. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, the president has some role. Typically, the president can choose the agency’s head subject to congressional approval, but the president can’t just go and fire officials that he doesn’t like for whatever reason or for no reason, because the agencies that operate the U.S. government and basically run our society are supposed to be professional. They’re supposed to be following their legal mandate. They’re not supposed to be personal tools of a dictator in the White House. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Well, the court just scrapped that. Now, lawyers, people who are legal experts, can do a better job of explaining just what went down. But what I think is important to understand is not only does this give essentially dictatorial powers to the occupant of the White House, but it also makes it extremely difficult for the economy to function. It makes it extremely difficult for society to function. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We live in a complicated world, a world of technology, where there are all kinds of spillovers, all kinds of ways in which it’s important that there be well-established ground rules. If you’re a business, take the example of medicines and foodstuffs, where we have an FDA, Federal Drug Administration, that is charged with ensuring that products that people consume are safe. We do that for very good reason. We know that not just that that there have been examples, historically, of products that were foods, medicines that were not at all safe, but also that people want some assurance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The fact that something has been FDA approved is a bit of a warranty, that it might turn out to be very harmful, but probably not. Businesses that want to invest in developing stuff need to know that there are some ground rules that determine what they can and cannot sell.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now imagine that all these decisions are made by political appointees who are loyalists to the president, who basically do whatever the president wants, whatever the people around the president want. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Do you want to invest in something where you have absolutely no idea what the ground rules will be, whether it will be approved or not? Do you want to invest in a whole business line when, for all you know, the White House will abruptly decide that your product isn’t safe and that a competitor’s product is, based on spurious grounds? </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And what would cause those decisions to happen? Well, how about the fact that some businesses are better at the business of bribing the president and his family than others. And if you think that this is outlandish — you know, a few years ago you might have said this was outlandish, things like that wouldn’t really happen — well, as we speak, these things are happening all the time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So you are setting up a situation in which, you know, it’s a little bit like traffic laws. Traffic laws, yeah, they can be annoying, but aren’t we all kind of glad that there are in fact rules about when you can turn and when you can go through an intersection? In order to function, in order to drive your car around you need to have a set of stable traffic rules, not a situation in which a police officer can decide you broke the law and the other guy did not because I say what the law is.  And especially not where the police officer does that based upon who’s been paying him off or who he expects to be paid off. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The real world is far more complex than traffic rules but we need those rules and we need some stability and those rules cannot be specified with every letter, every punctuation mark set by Congress. The world is too complicated and changes too much. You need to have standing ethos, standing doctrine at the agencies that make modern life possible. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now all of that is gone. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Now, it just adds to it that all of this is being done to empower a president who is the worst possible person for this job. This is not somebody you want supervising anything, everything that Trump touches turns to crud because he doesn’t care and he doesn’t actually understand or recognize that there’s such a thing as expertise as knowing what you’re doing. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So this would be terrible even if we had a temporarily competent administration. But now you’re doing all of this, the Supreme Court is doing all of this to empower the guy who brought you the Reflecting Pool, who brought you the Iran war. Utter nightmare. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, what will happen, hopefully, we emerge at the other end having fended off dictatorship. Then, I mean, as everybody knows, this Supreme Court is not actually empowering the presidency. It is empowering </span><em>this president.</em><span> And as soon as there’s a Democrat in the White House, suddenly there will be all kinds of restrictions on what that person can do. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Well, this cannot go on. This is a clear argument that says we have to one way or another disempower the Supreme Court. I don’t know enough to tell you what is the best route to do that but court packing or something else is going to have to happen. Because this has been the clearest signal yet that we have six people (there are three who are not part of it, but we have six people) who are fundamentally hostile to democracy, fundamentally hostile to the modern world and determined to put the catastrophically bad leader that we currently have sitting in the White House in charge of everything, which is a nightmare scenario on every level. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;">Take care, I guess.</p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman.
